title: Importation and Exportation of Goods
outcomes: Apply provisions on arrival of conveyances and manifests.
Apply bill of entry, assessment, payment and clearance rules.
Apply export, transit and transhipment provisions.
Compute duty on baggage under the Baggage Rules, 2026.

meta.exam_tip: Track the timeline: manifest, bill of entry, assessment, payment, out of charge — each has its own deadline.

concepts.title: Arrival of conveyances and manifests
body: Section 7 lets the Board appoint customs ports, airports, land customs stations, inland container depots, international courier terminals and foreign post offices. Under section 29, a conveyance from abroad must arrive only at such a customs port or airport unless forced elsewhere by accident, weather or similar compelling reasons.

Section 30: the person in charge of a vessel or aircraft must deliver the arrival or import manifest electronically before arrival, and of a vehicle, the import report within 12 hours of arrival. If delivered late without sufficient cause, the person responsible faces a penalty of up to ₹50,000.

Goods cannot be unloaded until entry inwards is granted (section 31) and only if listed in the manifest for that station (section 32). Unloaded goods remain with an approved custodian (section 45). Goods not cleared, warehoused or transhipped within 30 days of unloading (or extended time) may be sold by the custodian after notice to the importer (section 48).
concepts.work: A container left uncleared beyond 30 days can be auctioned after notice.

concepts.title: Bill of entry, assessment and clearance
body: Section 46: the importer files a bill of entry for home consumption or warehousing, electronically, before the end of the day (including holidays) preceding the day of arrival of the conveyance; the Board may allow later filing in specified cases, but not beyond the end of the day of arrival. Advance filing is allowed up to 30 days before expected arrival. Late filing without sufficient cause attracts charges of ₹5,000 a day for the first 3 days and ₹10,000 a day thereafter, not exceeding the duty payable, and capped at ₹50,000 where no duty is payable.

Section 17: the importer self-assesses duty; the proper officer may verify and reassess, and must pass a speaking order within 15 days if the importer does not accept the reassessment. Section 18 allows provisional assessment against security or bond where testing or documents are pending, with final assessment later.

Section 47(2): duty must be paid on the date of presenting a self-assessed bill of entry, or within one day (excluding holidays) of its return after assessment or reassessment; otherwise interest (currently 15% a year) runs till payment. Notified importers may pay on a deferred basis. On payment and checks, the officer issues an out-of-charge order for home consumption.
concepts.analogy: File early, pay the same day.
concepts.work: A bill of entry filed the day after arrival is already late under the current rule.

concepts.title: Export procedure, transit and transhipment
body: Exports need a shipping bill (by vessel or aircraft) or bill of export (by vehicle) under section 50, with a declaration of truth and documents. The exporter self-assesses export duty, if any. After assessment and examination, the proper officer gives a let export order under section 51, after which goods may be loaded.
Section 53 — transit: goods shown in the manifest as for transit in the same conveyance to a place outside India or to another customs station may pass without payment of duty, subject to rules.

Section 54 — transhipment: goods brought in for transhipment to another conveyance are allowed without duty on a bill of transhipment, when bound for a place outside India (or, under conditions, for another customs station in India).
concepts.analogy: Let export order is the green light to load.
concepts.work: Goods arriving at Mumbai on a ship bound for Colombo pass in transit without duty.

concepts.title: Baggage
body: Baggage is governed by sections 77 to 81 and the Baggage Rules, 2026, in force from 2 February 2026. All passengers, including infants, may clear used personal effects and travel souvenirs duty-free. General free allowance (arrival other than by land, not for infants): ₹75,000 for residents, tourists of Indian origin and foreigners on non-tourist visas; ₹25,000 for tourists of foreign origin. Land arrivals get only used personal effects. Allowances cannot be pooled.

Passengers aged 18 or more (other than crew) may bring one new laptop or notepad duty-free in addition. A resident or tourist of Indian origin who has lived abroad for over one year may bring jewellery up to 40 grams (female) or 20 grams (others) duty-free.

Transfer of residence for residents and tourists of Indian origin allows household and personal articles up to ₹1.5 lakh (3–12 months abroad), ₹3 lakh (at least one year in the preceding two years) or ₹7.5 lakh (at least two years abroad), with conditions. Unaccompanied baggage may arrive up to two months before the passenger (or one year where reasons are recorded). Goods beyond allowances attract duty at 35% ad valorem on the excess.
concepts.work: A resident bringing ₹70,000 of gifts by air pays no duty.

illustrations.title: Late bill of entry and late payment
illustrations.q: Tapti Polymers files a bill of entry 5 days after the due time without sufficient cause; duty payable is ₹7,30,000 (self-assessed). It pays the duty 10 days after presenting the bill of entry. A second consignment of exempt goods (no duty payable) is filed 8 days late. Compute late presentation charges for both and interest on the first.

checks.label: Late charges for 5 days of default: ₹5,000 × 3 + ₹10,000 × 2 (₹)
Late charges for 8 days where no duty is payable, capped at ₹50,000 (₹)
Interest at 15% p.a. on duty paid 10 days late (₹)

illustrations.title: Baggage of a returning resident
illustrations.q: Ritika, an Indian resident aged 30, returns by air from Singapore after a 10-day holiday with a new laptop (₹90,000) and a smartwatch and perfumes worth ₹1,10,000 together. Compute duty on her baggage, assuming the baggage rate of 35% ad valorem and ignoring any surcharge.

jobs.title: Import clearance planner
jobs.situation: A client's vessel arrives on Thursday.
steps: File the bill of entry by end of Wednesday.
Self-assess and pay duty the same day.
Track reassessment and reply within time.
jobs.takeaway: Advance filing avoids late charges and demurrage.

mcqs.q: Uncleared goods may be sold by the custodian after:
options: Thirty days from unloading, after notice

mcqs.q: Penalty for delay in delivering the import manifest can extend to:
mcqs.explain: Section 30(1). In practice: no sufficient cause.

mcqs.q: Loading of export goods is allowed after:
mcqs.explain: Section 51. In practice: out of charge.

mcqs.q: General free allowance for a tourist of foreign origin arriving by air is:
mcqs.explain: Baggage Rules 2026. In practice: not pooled.

summary: Section 30 manifest before arrival; penalty up to ₹50,000.
Section 46: BoE by end of day before arrival; late charges ₹5,000/₹10,000.
Section 48: sale after 30 days; sections 50–51 export; 53–54 transit/transhipment.
remember: Late charges capped at duty payable, or ₹50,000 where no duty.

viva.q: What happens if the importer disputes a reassessment?
viva.model: The proper officer must pass a speaking order within 15 days under section 17(5).
When documents or tests needed for final assessment are pending; the importer gives security or a bond under section 18.

viva.q: What is the difference between transit and transhipment?
viva.model: Transit goods stay on the same conveyance; transhipment goods move to another conveyance.

viva.q: Who may bring duty-free jewellery under the 2026 rules?
viva.model: A resident or tourist of Indian origin who has lived abroad for over one year, up to 40 grams for women and 20 grams for others.

viva.q: Can late presentation charges be waived?
viva.model: Yes, the proper officer may waive them if satisfied that there was sufficient cause for delay.

cases.title: Family returning from Dubai
cases.case: Aman (resident, 40), his wife Neha (resident, 36) and their son (1 year old) return by air after two years' work in Dubai. They carry used clothes, a new laptop each for Aman and Neha, Neha's jewellery of 35 grams and Aman's of 18 grams, and household goods worth ₹6 lakh. They did not claim transfer-of-residence relief earlier.

mcqs.explain: Abroad over one year. In practice: female limit.

mcqs.q: Household goods of ₹6 lakh under transfer of residence are:
mcqs.explain: Two years abroad. In practice: conditions apply.

mcqs.q: The infant's general free allowance is:
mcqs.explain: Infants excluded. In practice: personal effects free.

mcqs.q: How many laptops may come in duty-free?
options: Two — one each for Aman and Neha
mcqs.explain: One per adult passenger. In practice: 18 or above.
